common_name: Joanna Reed Catmint (Sturdy Long-Blooming Lavender-Blue Nepeta)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Joanna Reed was a top performer in the Chicago Botanic Garden's multi-year catmint trial for its unusually long, heavy bloom period and sturdy, non-flopping stems.

directions: Joanna Reed forms a broad, floriferous mound of gray-green, aromatic foliage topped from late spring through early fall with dense spikes of lavender-blue flowers, a bloom season notably longer than most catmint cultivars. Its thick, sturdy stems hold themselves upright through summer storms far better than many floppier Nepeta selections, so it rarely needs staking or a supporting grow-through ring. Shearing the plant back hard after the first flush of bloom in early summer keeps the clump dense and triggers a strong second wave of flowers into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained, average to lean soil; it is highly drought-tolerant and deer-resistant once established and draws bees steadily throughout its long season.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this species wants cooler, damper conditions than most catmints and performs best where summer heat and humidity are moderate.

directions: Unlike most catmints bred for hot, dry gardens, this Himalayan species wants cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil and tolerates significant afternoon shade, making it a useful choice for a partially shaded border or woodland edge where sun-loving Nepeta cultivars struggle. Loose, airy spikes of pale, creamy-yellow flowers rise well above the foliage from midsummer into early fall, a soft color unusual in a genus dominated by blue and violet tones. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and humid heat is moderate, tending to decline in hot, muggy climates without consistent moisture. Bees and other pollinators visit the flowers steadily, and its lax, slightly sprawling habit works well woven through part-shade perennial plantings rather than used as a tidy edging plant.

common_name: Peachie Keen Agastache (Compact Apricot-Peach Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Peachie Keen forms a dense, ball-shaped clump and needs excellent winter drainage to avoid crown rot.

directions: Peachie Keen forms a dense, rounded, ball-shaped clump of bright green, anise-scented foliage covered from midsummer into early fall with tightly packed spikes of soft apricot-peach flowers set off by contrasting purplish-pink calyxes. Its compact, self-supporting habit needs no staking and stays tidy without deadheading, fitting the front or middle of a sunny border, a large container, or a xeriscape planting. Plant in full sun in average to lean, very well-drained soil, since standing winter moisture is the most common cause of crown loss in agastache. Once established it is quite drought-tolerant and draws hummingbirds, bumble bees, and butterflies throughout its long bloom season.

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring in average, very well-drained soil in full sun; Apricot Sunrise is a hybrid hummingbird mint (Agastache coccinea x aurantiaca) that demands excellent drainage, especially over winter.

directions: Apricot Sunrise is a hybrid hummingbird mint (Agastache coccinea x aurantiaca) bearing tall, sinuous stems tinged dusty grape-purple and topped with slender spikes of deep orange buds that fade to a softer golden-apricot as they open, the whole spike set off by wine-purple calyxes. Its gray-green, licorice-scented foliage and long June-to-September bloom season make it one of the showiest agastache hybrids for a hot, sunny border, and it is an outstanding hummingbird plant. Plant in full sun in average, very well-drained soil; like other agastache it tolerates heat and dry spells well once established but is intolerant of wet feet, especially over winter. Leave the spent flower spikes standing into winter for seed-eating finches, then cut back hard in early spring as new basal growth begins.
